title: Every auth rate limit and brute-force lockout is keyed on a client-supplied header; the network control the code relies on is not in the deploy runbook
what: clientIp() returns `req.headers['x-real-ip']` with no trust boundary, falling back to `req.ip` (which, with `app.set('trust proxy', true)` in main.ts:35, is the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry — also client-supplied). Every unauthenticated auth budget is keyed on that value: `signup:ip:${ip}` / `login:ip:${ip}` / `pwreset:ip:${ip}` / `emailverify:ip:${ip}` (auth.controller.ts:135,167,251,282), `admin-login:ip:${ip}` (admin-auth.controller.ts:73), and the per-(account+IP) login lockout `login:fail:${uid}:${ip}` / `login:lock:${uid}:${ip}` (login.service.ts:15-16). The file's own comment says spoofing is impossible because "the host firewall only admits Cloudflare ranges, so the header cannot be spoofed by hitting the origin directly (see infra/caddy/Caddyfile)" — but infra/caddy/Caddyfile contains no `remote_ip` matcher or Cloudflare allowlist anywhere; it unconditionally does `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` (lines 177, 219, 276), i.e. it copies a header the client can set. The runbook the operator will actually follow, docs/deployment-hetzner.md:192-200, says `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp` — open to the entire internet, not Cloudflare ranges — and the same document warns that Docker-published ports bypass ufw regardless. Only the aspirational checklist in docs/server-handbook.md:891 mentions restricting 80/443, and it is a manual, unautomated, never-executed step on a box that has never been deployed to.
impact: An attacker rotating CF-Connecting-IP (or X-Forwarded-For) on requests sent straight to the origin gets unlimited attempts against every unauthenticated auth endpoint: unlimited password guessing against any known library account and against admin.libriant.com, unlimited signup (each of which provisions a Postgres database), unlimited password-reset email bombing. The per-account lockout never trips because a fresh bucket is created for every attempt. Every IP recorded in supportSession.ipAddress, supportRedemptionAttempt.ipAddress and the legal-consent record is attacker-authored fiction, which also breaks the GDPR accountability record signup.service.ts writes.
evidence: RAN (integration probe): sending `X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.9` with six wrong logins created the lock under exactly that attacker-chosen key — probe output `P9 redis lock key present = true` for key `login:lock:<uid>:198.51.100.9`. READ: `grep -rn 'remote_ip|trusted_proxies' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → no matches; `grep -n 'X-Real-IP' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` at 177/219/276 with no origin check. READ docs/deployment-hetzner.md:195-198 → `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp`.
fix: Do not trust the header unconditionally. In Caddy, wrap the reverse_proxy in a `@cf remote_ip <cloudflare-v4-and-v6-ranges>` matcher and `header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}` (not the client header) for anything that does not match; refuse or 403 non-Cloudflare origin traffic. In the app, replace `app.set('trust proxy', true)` with an explicit proxy list, and make clientIp() ignore X-Real-IP unless the immediate peer is a known proxy. Add the Cloudflare-range ufw rules to the actual deployment script (not only the checklist) and gate the deploy on an automated `nmap`/curl check that a direct-to-origin request with a forged CF-Connecting-IP does not reach the API.

title: Logout does not revoke the session — the JWT keeps working for up to 30 days, and there is no way to terminate a session at all
what: `POST /auth/logout` only calls `cookies.clearSession(res)`. It does not bump `users.sessionsValidAfter`, does not touch Redis, and the JWT carries no `jti` — there is no server-side session record of any kind. The only revocation primitive in the system is the account-wide `sessionsValidAfter` epoch, which is written solely by a password reset, an admin-forced reset, `completeSetup` with a new password, and deactivation. Consequently a session token that was captured before logout stays valid for its full TTL: 7 days by default, 30 days for a "remember me" login (`SESSION_REMEMBER_TTL_SEC` default 30d, env.ts:292), and sliding re-issue on every GET past half-life (session.middleware.ts:52-70) keeps refreshing it up to the 90-day absolute cap. There is no "sign out of all devices" endpoint and no session list.
impact: On the exact machines this product targets — the shared circulation desk that cookie.service.ts:22-27 explicitly designs for — clicking "Sign out" gives the user a false guarantee. Anyone who captured the cookie (shared browser profile, XSS-free but disk-resident cookie jar, backup, stolen laptop, malware) retains full library access for weeks, and the librarian has no action available that stops it short of performing a password reset they have no reason to think they need. A signup issues `remember: true` unconditionally (signup.service.ts:230), so owners are always on the 30-day token.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P1): `POST /auth/logout` with the owner cookie returned 204; re-presenting the same cookie to `GET /auth/me` returned **200** with the full user + tenant payload. Probe output: `P1 /auth/me after logout -> 200`.
fix: Give the token a `jti` and, on logout, write a Redis denylist entry `session:revoked:<jti>` with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime, checked in AuthGuard and TenantGuard alongside the existing `sessionsValidAfter` check. Add `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all` that bumps `sessionsValidAfter` and calls `AuthGuard.invalidateAuthCache`, and surface it in the UI as "Sign out everywhere".

title: Any unauthenticated caller can lock every Libriant admin out of the control plane, and doing so also kills their already-active sessions
what: `AdminAuthService.recordFailure` increments `adminUser.failedAttempts` and, at `MAX_FAILED_LOGINS` (default 5), sets `lockedUntil = now + LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS` **and** `status = 'locked'`. The lock is keyed on the account alone — there is no IP component, unlike the tenant side, where login.service.ts:10-16 documents exactly this attack ("A bare-account lock lets ANY attacker lock ANY user out … a trivial, renewable DoS") and fixes it with per-(account+IP) keys. Worse, `AdminAuthGuard.canActivate` rejects on `admin.status !== 'active'`, so flipping status to 'locked' does not merely block new sign-ins: it 403s the admin's **existing, valid session cookie** on the next request. Nothing in the app can clear the lock except a successful login (`recordSuccess` restores `status: 'active'`), which the attacker prevents by re-locking. The only per-IP brake is 20 admin-login attempts / 5 min (admin-auth.controller.ts:54) — and per authn-authz-01 that bucket is itself attacker-controlled.
impact: Five HTTP requests every fifteen minutes, from an unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses an admin email address, permanently deny the operator access to admin.libriant.com. There is no in-app unlock (no owner-tier unlock endpoint exists) — recovery requires direct database access. The likely moment for this attack is during an incident, when the admin console is exactly what is needed. It also blocks the support-key redemption path, so no engineer can reach a customer's library either.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P4): created an active admin, logged in (`/admin/auth/me` → 200), then sent five wrong-password logins from an unauthenticated client. DB row afterwards: `{"status":"locked","lockedUntil":"2026-08-23T10:02:37.603Z","failedAttempts":5}`. The previously-issued admin cookie then returned **403** `{"message":"Your admin account is no longer active."}`, and a legitimate re-login with the correct password returned **401**. Probe output lines P4.
fix: Key the admin lockout on (adminId, clientIp) in Redis the way LoginService already does, and stop writing `status = 'locked'` — the status column is read by AdminAuthGuard as an account-disabled signal and must not be driven by unauthenticated input. Keep `lockedUntil` as the gate inside `verify()` only. Add an owner-tier unlock endpoint plus a `scripts/` unlock so recovery does not need psql.

title: Disabling a Libriant admin does not end their live impersonation session — they keep full write access to a customer's library
what: ImpersonationMiddleware validates the `supportSession` row (endedAt, expiresAt, tenantId, adminId) but never reads `adminUser` — it does not check `status`, `disabledAt`, or `sessionsValidAfter`. TenantGuard then short-circuits to `return true` on `req.impersonation` before any account check, and RolesGuard returns true unconditionally for impersonation. The admin session cookie is a separate credential with its own 1-hour TTL; the impersonation cookie is signed with `IMPERSONATION_SECRET` and lives for `SUPPORT_SESSION_TTL_SEC` (default 4 hours). So the only thing that ends impersonation is the support-session row itself, which nothing updates when an admin is offboarded. AdminAuthGuard's careful `disabledAt`/`status`/`sessionsValidAfter` re-read on every `/admin/*` request has no counterpart on the impersonation path.
impact: Offboarding a support engineer — the moment when revocation matters most — leaves them with up to four hours of unrestricted read and write access to a live customer library: member PII, loans, catalogue, staff credentials. The library's own "end support access" control still works, but the library has no reason to use it and no signal that the admin was terminated. Same hole applies to a compromised admin account: locking or deleting the adminUser row does nothing to an already-open session.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P7): opened a supportSession for an active admin, minted the impersonation cookie, confirmed `GET /t/<slug>/members` → 200. Then set the adminUser to `status:'disabled', disabledAt: now`. With the same cookie: `GET /t/<slug>/members` → **200**, and `POST /t/<slug>/members` (a write) → **201**. Probe output lines P7.
fix: In ImpersonationMiddleware, join the adminUser in the same query (`supportSession.findUnique({ include: { admin: { select: { status, disabledAt, sessionsValidAfter } } } })`) and refuse to attach `req.impersonation` when the admin is not active or the JWT `iat` predates `sessionsValidAfter`. Additionally, have the admin disable/lock path call `SupportSessionService.end(..., 'admin_ended')` for every open session held by that admin.

title: An impersonating admin can mint permanent tenant credentials, and the audit log the library sees does not show it
what: `RolesGuard.canActivate` begins with `if (req.impersonation) return true;` — the impersonation cookie satisfies every `@Roles(...)` and `@StaffWrite()` annotation in the tenant API without any tenant session. That includes `POST /t/:slug/staff/:id/reset-password`, whose response body contains the new plaintext temporary password, and `DELETE /t/:slug/support/keys/pending`, which lets the impersonator destroy the library's own key-management state. The support-access model's whole premise is a consented, time-boxed, library-revocable 4-hour window; a credential handed out inside that window outlives it indefinitely, because nothing ties `users.passwordHash` to the support session. Meanwhile `SupportAuditInterceptor` writes only `{ method, path, status }` — no request body, no response body, no target — so the row the library reads at `GET /t/:slug/support/sessions/log` says `POST /t/<slug>/staff/<id>/reset-password 200` and gives the library no way to know a working credential was disclosed, or to which account. The interceptor's own comment concedes before/after diffs are "TODO".
impact: A Libriant admin (support tier — `POST /admin/support/redeem` is behind AdminAuthGuard only, with no `@AdminRoles`) who is granted one 4-hour support window walks away with a working staff password for that library, usable forever from the normal login page, indistinguishable from a real staff sign-in. The library's audit trail shows the request but not the disclosure. Given the product is sold to Greek public libraries holding member PII, this defeats the consent model the feature exists to provide and is not detectable after the fact.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P10): with **only** an impersonation cookie for a `support`-role admin and no tenant session at all — `DELETE /t/<slug>/support/keys/pending` → **204**; `GET /t/<slug>/support/sessions/log` → 200; `GET /t/<slug>/staff` → 200; `POST /t/<slug>/staff/<id>/reset-password` → **200, TEMP PASSWORD DISCLOSED**. READ support-audit.interceptor.ts:43-50 — the log row carries only sessionId/method/path/status.
fix: Deny credential-minting and support-key routes under impersonation: replace the blanket `if (req.impersonation) return true` with an allowlist, or add an `@NotUnderImpersonation()` decorator applied to `staff/:id/reset-password`, `staff` create, `staff/:id/role`, `billing/*`, `exports`, and the whole LibrarySupportController. If support genuinely needs a password reset, make it force `mustChangeCredentials` AND set `sessionsValidAfter`, return no plaintext to the admin, and email the credential to the library owner instead. Extend the audit row with target type/id and a redacted body summary so the log is meaningful.

title: Three mutating tenant surfaces carry no role guard — the read-only `volunteer` role can upload and delete member photos, book covers and arbitrary files
what: `roles.decorator.ts:31-38` defines the policy explicitly: `StaffWrite()` is "the role set allowed to CREATE/EDIT/ARCHIVE core library data … Excludes `volunteer` — a deliberately limited role that may READ everything but must not mutate. Apply to every mutating handler." Three controllers with mutating handlers are annotated `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` only, with no RolesGuard and no `@Roles`/`@StaffWrite`: MemberPhotosController (`POST` and `DELETE /t/:slug/members/:id/photo`), CoversController (`POST` and `DELETE /t/:slug/catalog/books/:id/cover`), and StorageDemoController's `POST /t/:slug/storage/:resourceType` (arbitrary upload, up to `STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 25 MB). Note the same file gets it right for `DELETE .../storage/:resourceType/:filename` and `POST .../storage-admin/recompute`, which do carry `@Roles('owner','admin')` — so the omission is an oversight, not a decision. The delete paths call `storage.delete(...)`, which removes the underlying file, not just the reference.
impact: Any volunteer account — the role a library hands to a helper it does not fully trust — can permanently destroy every member photograph and every book cover in the library (irreversibly; the files are deleted, not soft-deleted), replace a member's photo with arbitrary content, and burn the tenant's storage quota with 25 MB uploads. Member photographs are personal data of library members, many of them minors in a school-library deployment; their deletion or substitution by a limited-rights account is both a data-integrity and a GDPR-accountability failure.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P3): created a `volunteer` staff account. Control: `POST /t/<slug>/members` (a `@StaffWrite()` route) → **403**, confirming the role is correctly limited elsewhere. Same volunteer cookie: `POST /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **201** `{"photoAssetRef":"members/…png"}`; `DELETE /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **200**. Probe output lines P3.
fix: Add `RolesGuard` and `@StaffWrite()` to the `@Post`/`@Delete` handlers in members/photos.controller.ts and catalog/covers.controller.ts, and to `POST /t/:slug/storage/:resourceType` in storage-demo.controller.ts. Then add a lint/CI check that fails any `@Post|@Put|@Patch|@Delete` handler on a `t/:slug/*` controller which resolves to no `@Roles`/`@StaffWrite` metadata — the enumeration above shows spot-checking is what let three slip through.

title: The forced first-login credential change is bypassable with an empty request body, leaving the admin-known temporary password valid forever
what: `CompleteSetupDto` makes both `fullName` and `newPassword` optional, and `LoginService.completeSetup` sets `mustChangeCredentials: false` unconditionally — the flag is cleared whether or not a password was supplied (`const data = { mustChangeCredentials: false }`, then `if (input.newPassword) { … }`). `POST /auth/complete-setup` requires only a live session, which the staff member already has from signing in with the temp password. So a single `POST /auth/complete-setup {}` clears the gate. The docstring calls this deliberate ("Either field may be omitted (\"keep the same\")"), but the effect is that the credential the creating admin generated, saw in plaintext (`staff.service.ts` returns `tempPassword`), and typed into a chat message is the account's permanent password, and `sessionsValidAfter` is never bumped, so nothing about the account changes.
impact: Every admin-created staff account can end up permanently authenticated by a 12-character password that at least one other person knows verbatim and that was very likely transmitted over WhatsApp/email. The library believes the forced-change screen guaranteed otherwise — the UI shows the prompt once and never again. An admin who is later demoted or leaves retains working credentials for every staff account they ever created.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P2): created a librarian, signed in with the temp password (`mustChangeCredentials: true` in the login response), then `POST /auth/complete-setup` with body `{}` → **200 {"ok":true}`. DB afterwards: `mustChangeCredentials = false`, `sessionsValidAfter = null`. Signing in again with the **original** temp password → **200**. Probe output lines P2.
fix: Make `newPassword` required in `CompleteSetupDto` when the user's `mustChangeCredentials` is true (or simply require it always on this endpoint — it exists only for the forced-change flow), and only clear the flag in the branch that actually wrote a new hash. Keep bumping `sessionsValidAfter` there, as the code already does.

title: Account email can be changed with no password step-up, no notice to the old address, and no session invalidation
what: `POST /auth/change-email` is behind `AuthGuard` alone. It takes only `{ newEmail }` — no current password, no TOTP, no re-authentication of any kind — and stages a change confirmed by a link sent **only to the new address**. `requestEmailChange` sends nothing to the old address. When the token is redeemed, `verify()` runs `updateMany({ where: { id, tenantId }, data: { email: p.email, emailVerifiedAt: new Date() } })`: it does not check that the account's email is still the one that was current when the change was staged, and it does not bump `sessionsValidAfter`. The account's password is unchanged, so the legitimate owner is not logged out and gets no signal at all.
impact: Chained with authn-authz-02 (a session cookie is never revocable by logout), a stolen or borrowed session on a shared circulation-desk browser converts into permanent account ownership: the attacker points the email at an address they control, confirms it from their own inbox, and then uses `POST /auth/password-reset/request` to obtain a password and lock the real owner out. For a tenant `owner` account that is the whole library — billing, staff, export of all member data. The victim's only notification is the reset email that arrives at an address they no longer control.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P5): `POST /auth/change-email` with the owner's session cookie and body `{"newEmail":"attacker-…@evil.test"}` and no password → **202 {"ok":true}`. READ email-verification.service.ts:197-228 — no credential check, no message to `user.email`; :144-158 — the apply step does not re-validate the prior address nor touch `sessionsValidAfter`.
fix: Require the current password (and TOTP once tenant MFA exists) in `ChangeEmailDto` and verify it in `requestEmailChange`. Send a plain-text security notice to the OLD address at staging time with a revoke link. Record the prior email in the token payload and refuse to apply the change if `user.email` no longer matches. Bump `sessionsValidAfter` when the change lands.

title: An already-enrolled admin's second factor can be silently replaced with no step-up — a stolen admin cookie is enough
what: `POST /admin/mfa/setup` and `POST /admin/mfa/verify` are behind `AdminAuthGuard` only. Neither checks whether the admin is already enrolled, and neither requires the current password or a code from the currently-registered authenticator. `verify` overwrites `mfaSecretCipher`/`mfaNonce`/`mfaKeyId` and sets `mfaEnabled: true` for whatever secret the caller just enrolled. There is no re-authentication gate anywhere on the admin surface: `AdminSessionService` mints a 1-hour cookie at login and nothing ever asks for credentials again inside that window. The controller docblock also advertises a `POST /admin/mfa/disable` route "exposed for completeness" that does not exist in the file — the documentation and the code disagree about the MFA surface.
impact: MFA is the control that stops a stolen admin password from yielding the control plane (admin-auth.controller.ts:87 — "a password alone must not yield the control plane") and is a hard precondition for redeeming support keys into customer libraries (admin-support.controller.ts:101). An attacker who obtains an admin session cookie for one hour — XSS on the admin origin, an unlocked laptop, a cookie exported from a browser profile — re-points the second factor to their own authenticator and converts a transient session into durable, MFA-blessed control-plane access, including impersonation into any customer library that issues a support key. The real admin discovers it only when their own code stops working.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P6): created an admin, logged in, set `mfaEnabled: true` on the row to simulate an enrolled admin, then called `POST /admin/mfa/setup` with only the session cookie → **200, NEW SECRET ISSUED**. Probe output line P6.
fix: Gate `/admin/mfa/setup` and `/admin/mfa/verify` behind a re-authentication step when `mfaEnabled` is already true: require the current password and a valid code from the existing secret (via `MfaService.verifyTokenOnce`) before issuing or persisting a replacement. Bump `adminUser.sessionsValidAfter` on any MFA change and email the admin. Delete the stale `disable` line from the docblock or implement it with the same step-up.

title: Tenant login lockout exists only in Redis and fails open; the documented database backstop is never written
what: `isLockedOut()` reads a Redis key and `catch { return false }` — a Redis error means not locked. `recordFailure()` wraps the whole lock write in `try/catch {}` — a Redis error means no lock is recorded. `RateLimitService.hit` fails open for every non-`signup:` bucket, and its comment justifies that with "Per-account lockout (LoginService) is the backstop". That backstop does not exist: `users.lockedUntil` is `select`-ed at login.service.ts:102 and never read, and the only writes to it anywhere in the codebase set it to `null` (login.service.ts:134, password-reset.service.ts:140, staff.service.ts:126). Nothing in the tenant auth path ever sets a non-null `lockedUntil`. So a Redis outage removes 100% of brute-force protection from `/auth/login` simultaneously at both layers, and a Redis restart/flush instantly clears every in-flight lock.
impact: During any Redis incident — the same Redis that also backs the rate limiter, the reset tokens and the auth revalidation cache — every library account on the platform is open to unlimited password guessing at bcrypt-cost-12 speed, with no counter anywhere and no log line indicating the protection is off. The failure is silent: the login endpoint keeps returning ordinary 401s. Reading the code, an operator would reasonably believe `users.lockedUntil` still holds the line.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P9): six wrong logins for one account from one IP → Redis lock key present = true, DB row `{"failedLogins":5,"lockedUntil":null,"status":"active"}`. Deleting the two Redis keys (equivalent to a flush/restart) and immediately logging in with the correct password → **200**. READ: `grep -n lockedUntil apps/api/src/auth/*.ts apps/api/src/staff/*.ts` returns only `lockedUntil: true` (a select) and three `lockedUntil: null` writes — no write ever sets a time.
fix: Persist the lockout: in `recordFailure`, atomically increment `failedLogins` and set `lockedUntil` in the same `user.update` once the threshold is reached, and have `login()` check the DB `lockedUntil` in addition to the Redis key. Keep Redis as the fast path. Either delete the false "backstop" claim from rate-limit.service.ts:38-42 or make it true.

title: Password-reset and email-verification tokens are stored in Redis in plaintext, keyed by the token itself
what: `const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` is used verbatim as the Redis key (`pwreset:<token>`, `emailverify:<token>`) with the user/tenant ids as the value. The bearer secret is therefore stored at rest exactly as it appears in the email link. Redis in the production compose (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:362) runs `redis:8-alpine` with no `requirepass`, on the internal Docker network; anything that can `docker exec` into the box, read a Redis dump, or reach 6379 from another container can `KEYS pwreset:*` and mint a password reset for any account. The 60-minute TTL bounds the exposure window but the tokens are continuously present in a busy deployment.
impact: Any read of Redis state — an operator, a compromised sidecar, a backup archive, a monitoring exporter — yields directly usable account-takeover tokens for every library that has requested a reset in the last hour, including tenant owners. This turns a read-only foothold into full tenant compromise with no further work.
evidence: READ password-reset.service.ts:70-77 (`const key = \`pwreset:${token}\`; await this.redis.client.set(key, JSON.stringify({uid, tid}), 'EX', 3600)`) and email-verification.service.ts:76-88 (same pattern). READ infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:362 — `image: redis:8-alpine`, no `requirepass` in the command.
fix: Store `sha256(token)` as the key and keep the plaintext only in the email — `getdel('pwreset:' + sha256(submitted))` preserves the existing atomic single-use claim with a one-line change. Also set `requirepass` on the production Redis.

title: Mandatory admin-MFA is bypassed by any request path that merely contains `/mfa/` or `/auth/` as a substring
what: `isMfaEnrollmentPath(path)` returns `path.includes('/mfa/') || path.includes('/auth/')`. It is a substring test on the whole request path, not an allowlist of the enrollment routes. Today only `/admin/mfa/*` and `/admin/auth/*` match, so the gate holds — but any future admin route whose path contains those segments anywhere (`/admin/tenants/:id/auth/...`, `/admin/settings/mfa/policy`, or a `:param` whose value is `auth`) silently escapes `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED` with no test to catch it. The guard is the only thing enforcing AUTH-06.
impact: A latent bypass of mandatory admin MFA that will be introduced by an ordinary, innocuous-looking route addition, with nothing in CI to notice. Not exploitable against the current route table.
evidence: READ admin-auth.guard.ts:76-78 — `return path.includes('/mfa/') || path.includes('/auth/');`. Enumerated the admin route table (`grep -n '@Controller|@Post|@Patch|@Put|@Delete' apps/api/src/**/*controller.ts`): no current route other than `admin/mfa/*` and `admin/auth/*` matches, so this is latent rather than live.
fix: Replace the substring test with an explicit set of exempt route paths (`/admin/mfa/status`, `/admin/mfa/setup`, `/admin/mfa/verify`, `/admin/auth/me`, `/admin/auth/logout`), or better, mark them with an `@MfaExempt()` decorator the guard reads via Reflector so exemption is opt-in at the handler.

title: SupportSessionGuard is dead code, and TenantGuard's comment claims it runs
what: `SupportSessionGuard` is provided and exported by SupportModule but is not referenced by a single `@UseGuards(...)` anywhere in the codebase. TenantGuard's comment states "`SupportSessionGuard` (run by the support interceptor) validates the session row separately" — no interceptor runs it; the only global interceptor is `SupportAuditInterceptor`, which writes an audit row and enforces nothing. The session-row validation that TenantGuard is relying on is in fact done by `ImpersonationMiddleware` (impersonation.middleware.ts:49-63), so there is no live hole — but the guard that the code documents as the enforcement point is inert, and anyone adding a route that reads `req.impersonation` without going through the middleware would inherit no check.
impact: No exploitable gap today. The risk is that a reviewer (or the previous audit) reads TenantGuard's comment, believes an independent guard validates the support session, and leaves the real check — a middleware that silently no-ops on any error path — unexamined.
evidence: RAN `grep -rn 'SupportSessionGuard' apps/api/src/ | grep -v 'support.module|support-session.guard.ts'` → three hits, all inside comments (tenant.guard.ts:46, impersonation-session.service.ts:6, impersonation.controller.ts:10). No `@UseGuards(SupportSessionGuard)` exists.
fix: Either apply `SupportSessionGuard` to the impersonation-reachable routes and delete the duplicate DB lookup from the middleware, or delete the guard and correct TenantGuard's comment to name ImpersonationMiddleware as the enforcement point.

title: The applicant-PII CSV export is behind AdminRolesGuard but carries no @AdminRoles, so any admin tier can pull it
what: `GET /admin/applications.csv` is annotated `@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)` with no `@AdminRoles(...)`. `AdminRolesGuard.canActivate` returns `true` immediately when no roles metadata is present (admin-roles.guard.ts:36), so the guard is a no-op here and the route is open to every authenticated admin including `support` tier. Every other owner-sensitive admin route in the tree (`admin/tenants/:id/delete`, `admin/exports`, `admin/plans/*`, `admin/system-mode/*`, `admin/subscriptions`, `admin/announcements/*`, `admin/library-requests/*/approve`) does carry `@AdminRoles('owner')`; the sibling admin export controller (`export/admin-export.controller.ts:64-65`) gates its download at owner. The CSV contains `contact_name`, `contact_email`, `phone`, `library_name`, `city` and free-text `message` for every prospect that used the public application form.
impact: Whole prospect list, with names, emails and phone numbers, exportable by the lowest admin tier. Minor at current headcount but it is a full personal-data export with no owner gate and no audit row, which is exactly the kind of thing a GDPR access review flags.
evidence: READ applications.controller.ts:117-118 (guards present, no `@AdminRoles`) plus admin-roles.guard.ts:36 (`if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;`). Cross-checked against the full route enumeration: every other mutating or PII-exporting admin route in the codebase names `@AdminRoles('owner')`.
fix: Add `@AdminRoles('owner')` to `exportCsv`, matching `admin-export.controller.ts`. Consider making `AdminRolesGuard` fail closed on `/admin/*` routes that lack metadata, so the default is restrictive rather than open.

title: The authentication core is almost entirely untested — no spec covers login lockout, password reset, the CSRF Origin check, cookie flags, MFA, or the impersonation lifecycle
what: The unit suite has specs for `jwt-session.service`, `email-verification.service`, `email-verified.guard`, `signup-consent`, `admin-roles.guard` and `support-rate-limit` — and nothing else in the auth/support tree. There is no spec for `login.service` (lockout, timing parity, tenant-status handling), `password-reset.service` (single-use, expiry, enumeration), `password.service`, `cookie.service` (the `__Host-` prefix and Secure/SameSite flags — nothing anywhere asserts them), `auth.guard` (the revalidation cache and revocation path), `session.middleware` (sliding re-issue), `origin-check.middleware` (the entire CSRF layer), `mfa.service`/`mfa.controller`, `admin-auth.guard`, `impersonation.middleware`, `support-key.service`, or `support-session.service`. The integration suite (9 files, 43 tests, all green) covers admin role guards, admin audit, cross-tenant isolation, desktop access, imports, library workflow and scheduled jobs. Its `setup.ts` explicitly turns OFF two of the controls in this dimension — `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true` and `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED=false` — with the comment "MFA enforcement has its own dedicated coverage"; no such coverage exists.
impact: Eight of the fourteen defects above were reachable with a single HTTP request against a booted app and none of them was caught, including a working logout that does not log you out. There is no regression net at all under the auth surface, so any fix applied to the findings above can silently regress. This is also the mechanism by which the 2026-06-21 pre-prod audit certified this code: the suite passes and asserts almost nothing about authentication.
evidence: RAN `find apps/api/src -name '*.spec.ts'` (47 files; six in auth/support, listed above) and `pnpm --filter @libriant/api exec vitest run --project integration` → `Test Files 9 passed (9) / Tests 43 passed (43)`. READ apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:15,22 — `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED ||= 'true'`, `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED ||= 'false'`. The probe spec written for this audit (10 tests, since removed) reproduced findings 02-10 against the live app.
fix: Add an `auth-security.spec.ts` to the integration project asserting, at minimum: logout invalidates the presented cookie; `complete-setup {}` is rejected while `mustChangeCredentials`; a volunteer is 403 on every mutating tenant route (enumerate them from the route table); five wrong admin passwords do not 403 a live admin session; an impersonation cookie stops working when its admin is disabled; the Set-Cookie header carries `__Host-`/Secure/HttpOnly under a production-like env; and a cross-site Origin is rejected. Run at least one integration file with the real rate limiter and MFA enforcement on.
